extracted_by: hand, T-0258 piece 1 — the Democrat read, November 1833 (Vol. I No. 1)
note: Vol. I No. 1, the first number of the first newspaper printed in Chicago, and the earliest contemporary document this project holds. Pages 1 and 4 are national and foreign reprint, poetry and miscellany and carry no town claim; the town is on page 2 (the editorial page: the population figure, the schooner, the school) and page 3 (the advertisements, the election notice, the marriages, the village ordinances and the paper's own imprint). THE COLUMNS ARE NOT INTERLEAVED IN THIS ISSUE — unusually — so `lines_of_claim` is the whole cited range on every claim and no claim carries `interleaved`. What this transcription does instead is DUPLICATE lines: the segmenter reads a printed line twice and sets both copies, several times per column. Duplicates are quoted as they stand and dropped in the normalized reading, which is said in each claim's note. THIS ISSUE CARRIES NO POST-OFFICE LETTER LIST. Swept for every form the Democrat uses elsewhere — 'list of letters', 'letters remaining', 'remaining in the post office', 'uncalled for', a signature ending 'P. M.' — for no hit; the only post office reference is c021, an advertiser to be enquired for there. Across the whole of T-0258's thirty issues only four carry a letter list (1834-01-28, 1834-02-04, 1834-04-23, 1834-04-30), so the ticket's census-proxy clause has nothing to bite on here and is met by demonstrating absence, as T-0261 met it for the American. THE SCAN RECORD IS SENIOR TO THIS TRANSCRIPTION AND SEVEN CLAIMS SAY SO. data/sources/chicago_democrat_1833_11_26.json was verified against the page images on 2026-08-10 and corrected on 2026-08-11; where it and the transcription disagree or where it can read type the transcription cannot, the claim carries `reading: scan_verified` and its note names what the scan supplied — c002 (the schooner's master), c006 (the tavern keeper), c011 (Philo Carpenter's name), c012 (Kimball's address), c019 (Goss & Cobb's address), c033 (the imprint). c022 is the converse and is worth as much: the record warns that a transcription of this issue read 'C. & L. Harmon' for 'C. & I. HARMON', and THIS transcription reads the I correctly, so the warning attaches to a different artefact. TWO ADVERTISERS THE SCAN RECORD DOES NOT ENUMERATE are added by this pass: C. H. Chapman (c008) and S. Foot (c016). THREE TRAPS ARE QUARANTINED AND NONE OF THEM IS CLAIMED: the stock engraving over the 'Two Buildings to Let' notice (c010), the pencilled 'S. W.' in the margin beside the imprint (c033), and the estray notices, which are county filings from Du Page and Walker's Grove and not Chicago (c031).

claims.notes: THE FIRE ORDINANCE, AND IT DESCRIBES THE HOUSES IT IS AFRAID OF. Read for what it assumes rather than what it forbids: Chicago's buildings in November 1833 are wooden, with wooden or lath-and-plaster partitions; they are heated by STOVES and not fireplaces; the stove pipe is run through a partition or out through the roof or the side wall rather than up a masonry chimney; and it must stand eighteen inches proud of the roof, guarded where it passes by stone-ware, brick, tin or sheet iron. That is a specification for the roofline of the whole town — a stove pipe, not a chimney stack — and it is the corporation's own, twenty months before the scene date. Hamilton as Clerk of the County Commissioners' Court. data/sources/chicago_democrat_1833_11_26.json is a scan-verified reading of this issue's page images and outranks the transcription (T-0258, ruling 2 run backwards). Its fourth correction turns on exactly this: these notices are county-clerk estray filings from Du Page and Walker's Grove, NOT Chicago, and they must not be read as evidence of a Chicago estray pen. They are extracted here for the SEVEN NAMES they mint — Harry Boardman, Richard M. Sweet, Thomas Parsons, Stephen M. Salisbury, Jeremiah Walker, Timothy J. Clark and James Walker — and for the appraisal figures, which price a horse in Cook County in 1833 at fifty-five dollars. The two notices share a column and the segmenter has duplicated the second's appraisal line; the quote carries the duplication and the normalized reading does not. Two names are left inside their transcription brackets in the normalized reading too, because the reading is genuinely uncertain and the marker is the honesty.

claims.notes: TWENTY-FIVE DOLLARS FOR TWO HORSES, AND A DESCRIPTION GOOD ENOUGH TO PAINT FROM. This is the closest thing in the issue to a portrait of a living animal that stood in the town: fourteen hands and sixteen hands, bay and light sorrel, switch tails, both shod, one branded C on the near cheek and shoulder, both natural trotters that will rack under the saddle. A reconstruction that puts horses in these streets has here a contemporary specification of what two of them looked like, from their owner. P. Maxwell is Dr. Philip Maxwell in later sources and the expansion is NOT made here — the type says 'P. MANWELL', an N for an X, and the surname is normalized only that far. The trade route is incidentally recorded: the sorrel bought at Springfield in Sangamon County, the bay lately owned near Danville.

claims.notes: THE STRONGEST SINGLE ADDRESS IN THE ISSUE, because it is the paper's own and the paper knew where it was. data/sources/chicago_democrat_1833_11_26.json is a scan-verified reading of this issue's page images and outranks the transcription (T-0258, ruling 2 run backwards). It calls this the strongest item the source holds and quotes it in full from the scan: 'in the building on the corner of South Water and Clark-streets'. NOTE PRECISELY WHAT IT SETTLES — the JUNCTION, not the corner. It says 'on the corner of' and which of the four corners is not in the sentence; Andreas's 'SW corner' remains a separate, later and weaker claim. THE THIRD TRAP IN THIS SOURCE SITS BESIDE THIS VERY PARAGRAPH: a later reader has pencilled 'S. W.' in the right margin of the advertisement page, level with the imprint, in cursive, outside the column rule. It is a gloss by somebody who had probably read Andreas; if it were ever transcribed as part of the page it would look like contemporary corroboration and would silently promote this position from inferred to documented on no evidence. It is not in this transcription and it is not in this claim. 'FOUR PAGES' is also here: 'printed on an imperial sheet' is what makes the issue four pages, which is how the scan set's three pages are known to be incomplete.
